title: Professional Project Organization
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of professional project organization and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Professional Project Organization is one step in Debugging, Testing, and Software Quality; errors, warnings, assertions and tests provide distinct signals. Reproducible failing cases help isolate defects. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Test expected behavior and edge cases, avoid leaking sensitive values in logs, and run checks in a clean environment. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Professional Project Organization
content_blocks.code:
safe_divide <- function(a, b) { if (b == 0) stop("b must not be zero"); a / b }
safe_divide(6, 2)
content_blocks.run_instructions: CodeLeaf does not provide an R runtime. This block is an inspectable reference example; execute it in a local R console or a reviewed R-aware environment. Static validation checks file structure, not R semantics.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No example is executed by this CodeLeaf lesson. For a local run, use synthetic data in a temporary working directory, avoid production credentials or destructive writes, and restart a clean R session to clear lesson objects.
content_blocks.limitations: Validate invalid inputs and return predictable errors instead of silent bad values. Verify the snippet and expected output with the supported R and package versions before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For professional project organization, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

content.task: Apply professional project organization to a small synthetic example. Start with organizing source code and data, predict the result, compare it with a local R run, test one edge or failure case, and document one limitation. For integrations or package-dependent topics, submit a safe verification plan rather than claiming the code ran.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the organizing source code and data idea in a minimal example or safe design sketch.
State the expected result before running the example.
Verify one relevant boundary, missing-value or failure case.
Record assumptions and one limitation of the result.
content.expected_output: A reproducible professional project organization example or design sketch with the expected result, one checked edge or failure case, and a stated limitation.
hints: Start with “Organizing Source Code and Data” and identify the input and output before coding.
Prefer a small repeatable test and capture the result before changing the implementation.
Test a boundary, missing, invalid or failure input relevant to this topic.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
